\chapter{The Sky and Its Lights}
\label{ch:sa-sky}
\hlchaptermodality{31}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name five things overhead in Sanskrit --- sky, moon, star, wind and snow --- and take apart the name of the mountain range built on the last of them.}

Complete SA-C31-snow and demonstrate the chapter promise.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[ākāśaḥ]{\sk{आकाशः} (ākāśaḥ) — the sky, open space}

\label{lesson:SA-C31-sky}



\begin{quote}
Before the new word: what did \emph{añjaliḥ} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{आकाशः}}
\textbf{\sk{आकाशः}} (\emph{ākāśaḥ}) — \textquotedblleft{}the sky, open space\textquotedblright{}.

\textbf{\sk{आकाशः}} is the openness overhead. It is built on a piece meaning \textquotedblleft{}to shine, to be visible\textquotedblright{}, with \textbf{\sk{आ}} in front — so the sky is named as the bright open place where things can be seen at all, rather than as a lid over the world.

This one stayed home. Hindi, Marathi, Bengali and Telugu all keep it as \emph{ākāś} or \emph{ākāśam}, and traders carried it east, where Malay and Indonesian say \emph{angkasa} for the sky to this day. Ends in \textbf{-\sk{अः}}, like \textbf{\sk{दीपः}} and \textbf{\sk{हस्तः}}.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
A new set of words, and the space that everything else in this chapter sits in.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{ākāśaḥ}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{añjaliḥ}, then \emph{ākāśaḥ}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \sk{आकाशः} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}the sky, open space\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[candraḥ]{\sk{चन्द्रः} (candraḥ) — the moon}

\label{lesson:SA-C31-moon}



\begin{quote}
Before the new word: what did \emph{ākāśaḥ} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{चन्द्रः}}
\textbf{\sk{चन्द्रः}} (\emph{candraḥ}) — \textquotedblleft{}the moon\textquotedblright{}.

Sanskrit names the moon by what it does: the root behind \textbf{\sk{चन्द्रः}} means \textquotedblleft{}to shine, to glitter\textquotedblright{}. The moon is simply the shining one.

Latin kept that root in \emph{candēre}, \textquotedblleft{}to glow white\textquotedblright{}, and English is full of its children — \emph{candle}, \emph{candid}, \emph{incandescent}, and the \emph{candidate}, who once wore a bleached white toga to be seen in a crowd. Sanskrit called the moon the glowing thing; Latin called a candle the same thing.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
A second word overhead, and a candle lit from the same root.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{candraḥ}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{ākāśaḥ}, then \emph{candraḥ}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \sk{चन्द्रः} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}the moon\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[tārā]{\sk{तारा} (tārā) — a star}

\label{lesson:SA-C31-star}



\begin{quote}
Before the new word: what did \emph{candraḥ} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{तारा}}
\textbf{\sk{तारा}} (\emph{tārā}) — \textquotedblleft{}a star\textquotedblright{}.

\textbf{\sk{तारा}} is a star, and it is among the most travelled words in the family. English \emph{star}, German \emph{Stern}, Latin \emph{stella}, Greek \emph{astēr} — behind \emph{astronomy} and \emph{asterisk} and \emph{disaster}, \textquotedblleft{}a bad star\textquotedblright{} — and Persian \emph{setāre} are all the same word, from a shape like \textbf{*ster-}.

Sanskrit dropped the \emph{s-} at the front and kept the rest. Ends in \textbf{-\sk{आ}}, like \textbf{\sk{माला}} and \textbf{\sk{यात्रा}}.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
A third light overhead, and a word that reached every branch of the family.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{tārā}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{tārā}, and one of its cousins outside India
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \sk{तारा} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a star\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[vāyuḥ]{\sk{वायुः} (vāyuḥ) — wind, air}

\label{lesson:SA-C31-wind}



\begin{quote}
Before the new word: what did \emph{tārā} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{वायुः}}
\textbf{\sk{वायुः}} (\emph{vāyuḥ}) — \textquotedblleft{}wind, air\textquotedblright{}.

\textbf{\sk{वायुः}} is the wind, and also the air it is made of. Its root means \textquotedblleft{}to blow\textquotedblright{}, so the word says what the thing does.

English \emph{wind} is the same word worn down, and so are German \emph{Wind}, Gothic \emph{winds} and Latin \emph{ventus}, which gives \emph{vent} and \emph{ventilate}. Ends in \emph{-uḥ}, the ending you had on \textbf{\sk{गुरुः}}.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
A fourth thing overhead — the one you feel rather than the one you look for.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{vāyuḥ}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{candraḥ}, \emph{tārā}, then \emph{vāyuḥ}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \sk{वायुः} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}wind, air\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[himam]{\sk{हिमम्} (himam) — snow, frost}

\label{lesson:SA-C31-snow}



\begin{quote}
Before the last word of the chapter: what did \emph{vāyuḥ} mean, and what did \emph{ākāśaḥ} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{हिमम्}}
\textbf{\sk{हिमम्}} (\emph{himam}) — \textquotedblleft{}snow, frost\textquotedblright{}.

\textbf{\sk{हिमम्}} is snow, and cold generally: the word covers the frost on a field and the season it belongs to.

Its cousins name the season rather than the snow: Greek \emph{kheimōn} and Latin \emph{hiems}, both \textquotedblleft{}winter\textquotedblright{}, the second giving English \emph{hibernate}. And the mountains carry it: \emph{Himālaya} is \textbf{\sk{हिमम्}} joined to \emph{ālaya}, \textquotedblleft{}a dwelling\textquotedblright{} — the abode of snow. Neuter \textbf{-\sk{अम्}}, like \textbf{\sk{वस्त्रम्}}.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Five things overhead, and a mountain range whose name you can now take apart.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{himam}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item all five in order, then say what \emph{Himālaya} means
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \sk{हिमम्} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}snow, frost\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
